title: Why Are We Still Leaving Mentors to Figure It Out?
author: Dr Haili Hughes
summary: Hughes argues that schools routinely assume good teachers will make good mentors without any deliberate preparation for the role, an assumption she says is false. Drawing on her own experience developing mentors across England, including work on ITT reaccreditation for the Department for Education, she contends that mentoring is a distinct professional skill requiring both technical knowledge (observing, giving feedback, bridging university learning and classroom reality) and relational qualities like empathy, trust-building and emotional intelligence. She stresses that mentoring also benefits the mentor, sharpening their own reflective practice and professional identity. The piece closes with a structural argument aimed at school leaders: training alone cannot work without protected time, manageable workloads and sustained organisational commitment to developing mentors rather than simply appointing them.
points: Hughes reframes mentor quality as a retention lever, arguing that a skilled mentor can determine whether a new teacher stays in the profession at all.
She distinguishes technical mentoring skill (observation, feedback, problem-solving) from relational skill (listening, trust, psychological safety), insisting both must be taught rather than assumed.
Her claim that mentoring is 'professional learning for themselves' reframes mentor training as a two-way developmental investment, not a one-way service to novices.
She places responsibility on schools, not just individual mentors, arguing that protected time and leadership support are preconditions for mentoring to succeed.
quotes: Some of the finest classroom practitioners I've worked with have admitted they felt completely unprepared when asked to mentor a beginning teacher. They cared deeply. They wanted to help. But knowing how to teach children is not the same as knowing how to develop another adult's professional practice.

Mentors consistently say they want usable strategies they can take straight back into school. They need to know how to observe lessons with purpose, guide classroom practice, give constructive feedback and help novice teachers solve the everyday problems that inevitably arise during the first year.

That is why mentor preparation needs to include emotional intelligence alongside instructional knowledge. It should help mentors learn how to listen actively, build trust, conduct non-judgemental conversations and create psychologically safe relationships where honest reflection can flourish.

Schools need to create the conditions in which mentoring can succeed. That means protected time, manageable workloads, clear expectations, leadership support, opportunities for mentors to learn from one another and access to appropriate resources.

If we genuinely believe that beginning teachers deserve high-quality support, then we must stop treating mentoring as an extra duty assigned to experienced teachers. It is a specialist professional practice that requires deliberate preparation, ongoing learning and organisational commitment.
